

---

## 3️⃣ Submit the job

### **If you use Slurm**

```bash
# Request 16 GPUs on a single node (or 2 nodes × 8 GPUs each)
# -N 1   → one node (change to 2 if you need multiple nodes)
# -G 16  → 16 GPUs
# -t 2:00:00 → 2‑hour time limit
# -J eval_job   → job name (helps with monitoring)
# -o slurm_%j.out -e slurm_%j.err → stdout/stderr files
# -A <account>  → your allocation/account (if required)

sbatch -N 1 -G 16 -t 2:00:00 -J eval_job \
       -o slurm_%j.out -e slurm_%j.err \
       ./eval_job.sh
```

If you prefer an interactive allocation (e.g., to run a container manually):

```bash
srun -N 1 -G 16 -t 2:00:00 \
     ./eval_job.sh
```

```bash
# -l nodes=1:ppn=16:gpus=16   → 1 node, 16 GPUs
# -l walltime=02:00:00        → 2‑hour limit
# -N eval_job                 → job name
# -j oe                       → join stdout/stderr
# -o /path/to/stdout.log      → optional separate file
```

Replace `<JOBID>` with the number printed by the submit command (e.g., `1234`).

| Red Flag | Why It’s Suspicious |
|----------|--------------------|
| **Urgency or fear** – “Your account will be closed tomorrow!” | Attackers want you to act before you think. |
| **Unexpected reward** – “You’ve won a $500 gift card!” | Lures you into clicking a link or opening an attachment. |
| **Generic or vague** – “Important notice” or “Hello” | Legitimate organizations usually address you by name. |
| **Spelling/grammar errors** – “Your account has been suspened” | Many phishers rush and make mistakes. |

---

## 2. The Sender – Look Closer Than the Display Name

| What to Check | How to Verify |
|---------------|---------------|
| **Display name vs. email address** – “HR Department <hr@company.com>” vs. “HR Department <hr‑alerts@company‑services.com>” | Hover over the sender’s name to see the actual email address. |
| **Domain mismatch** – “@paypa1.com” (notice the “1” instead of “l”) | Compare the domain to the official one (e.g., “paypal.com”). |
| **Unexpected sender** – A message from a senior exec you don’t usually hear from | Verify through a separate channel (phone, Teams, in‑person). |

---

## 3. Greeting & Tone

| Red Flag | Why It’s Suspicious |
|----------|--------------------|
| **Generic greeting** – “Dear Customer,” “Hello,” “Hi there” | Legitimate internal communications usually use your name. |
| **Overly formal or overly casual tone** that doesn’t match the sender’s usual style | Phishers often copy/paste language from different sources. |
| **Requests for personal info** – “Please confirm your SSN, password, or credit‑card number” | Reputable companies never ask for sensitive data via email. |

## 4. Content – The Hook

| Common Hook | What to Look For |
|-------------|-----------------|
| **“Verify your account” or “Security alert”** | Look for a link that doesn’t match the official site (hover to see the URL). |
| **“Invoice attached” or “Document for review”** | Check the attachment type – unexpected PDFs, ZIPs, or executables are risky. |
| **“Click here to reset your password”** | Hover over the button; the URL should be HTTPS and match the brand exactly. |
| **“Urgent request from the CEO”** | Verify the request through a separate channel before sending any money or data. |

---

## 5. Visual & Formatting Clues

| Red Flag | Why It’s Suspicious |
|----------|--------------------|
| **Mismatched logos or branding** – low‑resolution images, wrong colors | Phishers often copy logos from the web but get details wrong. |
| **Inconsistent fonts or spacing** | A quick copy‑paste can leave formatting glitches. |
| **“Reply‑to” address that’s different from the sender** | Used to route responses to the attacker. |

---

## 6. Links & Attachments – The Real Threat

| What to Do | How to Do It |
|------------|--------------|
| **Hover before you click** – Look at the full URL in the tooltip or status bar. | Does it match the sender’s domain? Is it HTTPS? |
| **Check the domain** – “login.paypal.com” vs. “login.paypal.com‑secure.com” | Even a single extra character can be a trap. |
| **Don’t open unexpected attachments** – Especially .exe, .zip, .scr, or macros in Office files. | If you must, open in a sandboxed environment or ask IT. |
| **Verify the link in a new browser** – Type the official URL manually instead of clicking. | This bypasses any malicious redirect. |

---

## 7. Social‑Engineering Tactics to Watch

| Tactic | Example |
|--------|---------|
| **Authority** – “From the CFO, urgent wire transfer request” | Verify the request via phone or in‑person. |
| **Familiarity** – Uses names of coworkers, projects, or internal jargon | Still verify; attackers often harvest internal details from social media. |
